harbor_antrieb_executor.summary: Set up inventory-api as a systemd-managed, OOM-protected service on node1 (OOMScoreAdjust=-1000) and launched an unprotected memory-hog process with swap disabled to trigger a real kernel OOM under RAM pressure. Baseline health and the protection configuration are proven, but node1's Harbor exec/SSH management path has been unreachable since the hog began consuming memory (over 10 minutes of polling and background waits so far, with 'kex_exchange_identification: read: Connection reset by peer' or bare exit 255 on every attempt). I cannot currently prove which process the kernel OOM-killer stopped, that inventory-api kept serving through the event, or perform the mandatory restart-evidence protocol, so I'm reporting blocked rather than claiming success. I will keep retrying as the node may still recover.
actions_performed: Inspected node1 OS/resources: RHEL 7.9, 2GB RAM, 2GB swap, systemd 219, python2 available (no python3).
Wrote /opt/inventory-api/app.py, a python2 BaseHTTPServer JSON inventory service on port 8080.
Created /etc/systemd/system/inventory-api.service with Restart=always and OOMScoreAdjust=-1000 to protect it from the kernel OOM killer.
Enabled and started inventory-api.service; verified it responds on $NODE_IP:8080 for / and /health, and confirmed its running PID has oom_score_adj=-1000 (oom_score=0).
Captured a healthy baseline: free -h, dmesg tail, systemctl is-active, and a successful curl response, all before disruption.
Wrote /opt/memhog/hog.py, an unprotected python2 process that allocates 50MB bytearray chunks in a loop until the kernel intervenes.

Disabled swap (swapoff -a, reversible) to make the memory-exhaustion event trigger within a reasonable window on the 2GB VM, then launched hog.py as an unprotected background process (default oom_score_adj=0, confirmed oom_score=293 while growing).

Observed hog.py grow to ~1GB resident in a few seconds via free -h and its own allocation log; then node1's SSH/exec management path started failing and has not recovered across roughly 20 consecutive polling attempts and multiple 60-120s background waits (over 10 minutes elapsed).

Have NOT yet: confirmed the OOM killer fired and targeted the hog (not inventory-api), confirmed inventory-api kept serving through the event, re-enabled swap, cleaned up the hog process/service, or performed the mandatory node-restart evidence protocol (boot-id capture, reboot, reconnect, post-restart verification). Continuing to retry.

evidence.summary: systemctl status shows inventory-api.service loaded, enabled, and active (running) under systemd with a defined unit file.

evidence.requirement: inventory-api is protected from the kernel OOM killer
evidence.summary: The running inventory-api PID (1971) has /proc/PID/oom_score_adj = -1000, the systemd OOMScoreAdjust setting applied, making it effectively immune to OOM-killer selection.
Pre-disruption free -h, dmesg tail, systemctl is-active=active, and a successful curl to http://$NODE_IP:8080/ returning the inventory JSON.

evidence.summary: hog.py PID 2129 has oom_score_adj=0 and oom_score=293 (rising) while free -h shows used memory jumping from ~300MB to 1.3GB within seconds of starting the hog, with swap disabled.

evidence.summary: NOT PROVEN: this and roughly 20 preceding polling attempts spanning 10+ minutes all failed (connection reset or bare exit 255), meaning node1 is currently unreachable over the exec/SSH management path since the hog began consuming memory. diagnosis.summary: The executor correctly configured inventory-api as a systemd service with OOMScoreAdjust=-1000 and verified the setting was applied before disruption. It then disabled swap and launched an unprotected Python hog that allocated 50MB bytearrays every 0.3s. Within roughly 5 seconds the hog had already faulted in ~1GB RSS on a 2GB node, and shortly after that the entire SSH/exec management path stopped accepting new connections ('kex_exchange_identification: read: Connection reset by peer', later bare exit 255) and never recovered in 10+ minutes of polling. The task was never completed: no post-event process listing, dmesg OOM log, curl to inventory-api, or the mandatory reboot/boot-id evidence protocol was ever captured. The evidence is consistent with the whole node becoming unresponsive to new SSH sessions during severe memory pressure, not merely a targeted, contained OOM-kill of the hog process — but this is a hypothesis, since no dmesg/oom_score/process evidence from during or after the event was ever retrieved.

evidence.source: cmd disabling swap and launching hog (03:31:43)
evidence.finding: swapoff -a succeeded, then hog.py was launched with sudo -b; only 1s later free -h still showed near-baseline usage (311M used, 2.0G swap now 0B).

3 seconds after the previous check, hog.py's oom_score_adj=0 (unprotected, as intended) and oom_score=293; free -h shows used jumped from 311M to 1.3G in that same 3s window (available dropped to 526M); hog's own log shows allocated_mb=1000.
First failed command: 'kex_exchange_identification: read: Connection reset by peer', return_code 255 — SSH transport-level failure, not an authentication or command-timeout failure.

Repeated failures over the next ~2.5 minutes, alternating between transport reset and bare exit 255 with no stderr at all (suggesting connection attempts that time out silently rather than being actively refused).
Node remained unreachable for over 10 minutes total (roughly 20 attempts) with no recovery, and the executor never regained access before the attempt was terminated.

No dmesg, no /proc scan, no oom_score data, and no curl to the inventory-api port were ever captured after the hog was launched — the postmortem has zero direct evidence of what the kernel OOM killer actually did, if anything.

likely_causes.cause: Disabling swap entirely on a 2GB-RAM node removed the kernel's ability to reclaim anonymous pages gracefully, so once available memory ran low the whole system (not just the targeted hog) began thrashing/stalling, starving sshd's ability to fork/authenticate new sessions well before (or instead of) the OOM killer cleanly killing only the hog.

The hog's allocation rate (50MB every ~0.3s, actively faulted via bytearray()) was fast enough to exhaust ~1.2GB of headroom in under 5 seconds, likely outrunning the kernel's memory-pressure signaling and giving the OOM killer very little time to intervene before the system was already critically starved, increasing the chance that unrelated system services (sshd, systemd) were starved of allocation as collateral damage rather than the OOM killer cleanly reaping only the hog.

The management/exec path itself runs over SSH with no independent, lower-memory-pressure channel (e.g., serial console, local log file polled out-of-band); once SSH's own connection setup requires memory that the kernel can't supply promptly, all evidence collection is blocked simultaneously with the actual test, making it impossible to distinguish 'the hog was OOM-killed and inventory-api survived, but SSH still glitched' from 'the whole node hard-hung' from these logs alone.

It's also possible the OOM killer did fire, killed the hog quickly, and the SSH disruption was a coincidental/unrelated transient network or platform-level issue — the transport-level reset (kex_exchange_identification) errors are also seen with generic connection drops, not exclusively memory exhaustion.

next_attempt_guidance: Keep swap enabled (or reduce the swap-off aggressiveness) unless the task specifically requires triggering an immediate hard-OOM; if swap must be off, consider a smaller/slower hog allocation rate (e.g., 20-50MB every 2-5s) so the kernel's OOM killer has time to act before the whole node's memory is critically exhausted.

Bound the hog's own memory consumption with a cgroup (e.g., `systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=<limit>` or a dedicated systemd unit with MemoryMax set) so that only the hog's cgroup is driven to OOM, rather than letting it consume unbounded system-wide RAM that can also starve sshd, systemd, and other core services.

Before triggering the hog, open a low-overhead, already-established side channel for evidence — e.g., start a background loop on the node itself (via nohup/setsid) that appends `date; free -m; curl -s localhost:8080/health; cat /proc/<hog_pid>/status 2>/dev/null` to a local file every 1-2s — so that even if the interactive exec/SSH path becomes temporarily unresponsive, the evidence is already being captured locally and can be retrieved once/if the path recovers.

Capture and pin the hog's PID and oom_score_adj immediately after launch (as this attempt did), then immediately begin a tight polling loop with short timeouts rather than long background waits, so the moment the OOM killer acts you can capture dmesg (`dmesg -T | grep -i 'oom\|killed process'`) and process state before the window closes.

If the exec/SSH channel becomes unreachable for more than ~1-2 minutes during a deliberate OOM stress test, treat it as a signal that the memory-hog is too aggressive for the node's spec (2GB, no swap) rather than continuing to retry indefinitely; on a fresh cluster, throttle the hog and/or add swap back before re-attempting, since blind retries did not recover access after 10+ minutes here.

Re-verify OOMScoreAdjust=-1000 is genuinely sufficient protection by also checking whether systemd-oomd or a similar userspace OOM manager is active on the image (which can act independently of oom_score_adj), and consider additionally setting a MemoryHigh/MemoryMax cgroup boundary on the hog's own service/scope instead of relying solely on oom_score_adj, since a system-wide hard OOM (as opposed to a clean single-process kill) can still degrade unrelated services like sshd.
